core_instruments.name: UNGA Resolution 76/300 (2022)
core_instruments.title: Right to a Clean, Healthy and Sustainable Environment
core_instruments.summary: Recognises that a clean, healthy and sustainable environment is a universal human right. Air pollution is a direct violation of this right for hundreds of millions of people.
core_instruments.relevance: Provides the strongest global normative foundation for treating clean air as a justiciable right.

core_instruments.name: Paris Agreement (2015)
core_instruments.title: Climate Action & Equity
core_instruments.summary: Commits parties to limit warming and to pursue efforts to 1.5°C, while recognising equity and common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR-RC).
core_instruments.relevance: Air pollution co-benefits of climate mitigation are explicitly recognised; fossil-fuel combustion drives both climate change and lethal particulate pollution.

core_instruments.name: UNFCCC
core_instruments.title: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
core_instruments.summary: The parent treaty establishing the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.
core_instruments.relevance: Frames why historically high-emitting nations and actors bear greater responsibility for both climate and air-quality harm.

core_instruments.name: Aarhus Convention principles
core_instruments.title: Access to Information, Public Participation & Justice
core_instruments.summary: Although regional, its three pillars (information, participation, justice) are widely cited as global best practice for environmental democracy.
core_instruments.relevance: Community reporting and transparent air-quality data are practical expressions of the right to environmental information.

core_instruments.name: Polluter Pays Principle
core_instruments.title: Rio Declaration Principle 16
core_instruments.summary: The polluter should bear the cost of pollution, with due regard to the public interest and without distorting international trade.
core_instruments.relevance: Supports accountability for industrial, transport and open-burning sources of local air pollution.

climate_justice_pillars.title: Distributive Justice
climate_justice_pillars.text: The poorest communities and Global South cities often breathe the most polluted air while having contributed least to the emissions causing the problem.

climate_justice_pillars.title: Procedural Justice
climate_justice_pillars.text: Affected people must have meaningful access to information, decision-making processes, and remedies — not merely be subjects of monitoring.

climate_justice_pillars.title: Intergenerational Justice
climate_justice_pillars.text: Children and future generations inherit both the climate system and the cumulative health burden of chronic exposure to polluted air.

climate_justice_pillars.title: Recognition Justice
climate_justice_pillars.text: Informal workers, outdoor labourers, women cooking with solid fuels, and residents of informal settlements are systematically under-counted in official data.

key_facts: Air pollution is responsible for an estimated 7 million premature deaths every year (WHO).
More than 90% of the world’s population breathes air that exceeds WHO guideline limits.
The health burden falls disproportionately on low- and middle-income countries.
Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is both a major climate forcer and the leading environmental risk factor for premature death.
The right to a clean environment was recognised by the UN General Assembly in 2022 as a human right.
